\chapter{Blood and Household --- Son, Daughter, Grandfather, Grandmother, Husband}
\label{ch:hijos-y-abuelos}
\hlchaptermodality{306}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the closest members of a family in Spanish --- son, daughter, grandfather, grandmother and husband --- and switch the ending to say which one I mean.}

Complete ES-C306-esposo: name all five relatives, taking the -o/-a switch in both directions.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el hijo]{el hijo --- the f that turned into a silent h}

\label{lesson:ES-C306-hijo}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el hijo} --- \textquotedblleft{}the son.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{filius}. English kept it in the borrowed words rather than the everyday one: \emph{filial} duty is the duty owed by a son or a daughter, and to \emph{affiliate} is to take something in as a son.

Spanish did something to it that English never did. A Latin \textbf{f-} at the front of a word became Spanish \textbf{h-}, and then that h- fell silent. \emph{Filius} became \emph{hijo}: the letter is written and never said.

Once you have seen the rule it keeps paying out --- \emph{facere} became \emph{hacer}, \emph{ferrum} became \emph{hierro}, \emph{fumus} became \emph{humo}. The h you do not pronounce is the fossil of an f.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first person most people name after they have given their own name.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el hijo}
  \item \emph{el nombre del hijo}
  \item \emph{mi hijo, señor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{hijo} in Latin? (\emph{Filius}.) Which English words still show that f? (\emph{Filial}, \emph{affiliate}.) Do you say the h? (No --- never.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la hija]{la hija --- the same root, the other ending}

\label{lesson:ES-C306-hija}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la hija} --- \textquotedblleft{}the daughter.\textquotedblright{}

Same Latin root, feminine end: \textbf{filia} beside \textbf{filius}. Spanish did not need a second word, only a second vowel. You have met this machinery already with \emph{contento} and \emph{contenta} --- here it does the work of a whole separate noun.

English has no everyday cousin either, so it leans on the same borrowed \emph{filial}, which quietly covers sons and daughters at once.

There is one more place the root is hiding. A Spanish \textbf{hidalgo} --- the minor nobleman --- is a worn-down \emph{hijo de algo}, \textquotedblleft{}son of something,\textquotedblright{} meaning son of somebody with property. The rank is a description of a parent.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A pair: change the last vowel, change who you are talking about.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la hija}
  \item \emph{el hijo y la hija}
  \item \emph{el nombre de la hija, por favor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the only difference between \emph{hijo} and \emph{hija}? (The last vowel.) What is an \emph{hidalgo} literally? (\emph{Hijo de algo} --- son of something.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el abuelo]{el abuelo --- the little grandfather}

\label{lesson:ES-C306-abuelo}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el abuelo} --- \textquotedblleft{}the grandfather.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{avus} was the grandfather. Spanish did not inherit \emph{avus} plainly; it inherited the fond diminutive \textbf{aviolus}, \textquotedblleft{}the little grandfather,\textquotedblright{} and wore it down to \emph{abuelo}. The affection is baked into the word.

English holds the same root in two long words. \emph{Avuncular} --- warm in the way an uncle is warm --- comes from \emph{avunculus}, which is itself \textquotedblleft{}little grandfather\textquotedblright{} and drifted to mean the mother's brother. And \emph{atavistic}, a trait surfacing from far back, is \emph{atavus}, an ancestor several grandfathers deep.

Notice what that means: English \emph{uncle} is a worn-down \emph{avunculus}. Your word for grandfather and their word for uncle are the same Latin word, pulled two ways.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A root that runs through two English words most people never connect.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el abuelo}
  \item \emph{el abuelo y el hijo}
  \item \emph{el apellido del abuelo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{avus}? (Grandfather.) Why is \emph{avuncular} about uncles? (\emph{Avunculus}, little grandfather, drifted to mother's brother.) What does \emph{atavistic} reach back to? (A distant ancestor.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la abuela]{la abuela --- twice over, and again}

\label{lesson:ES-C306-abuela}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la abuela} --- \textquotedblleft{}the grandmother.\textquotedblright{}

The switch you have now done twice: \emph{abuelo} to \emph{abuela}. Third time you have met this ending doing the work of a separate word, and it will not be the last.

Spanish then does something tidy that English handles with a hyphen. Stack the Latin \textbf{bis}, \textquotedblleft{}twice,\textquotedblright{} on the front and you get \emph{bisabuela} --- the great-grandmother, the grandmother twice over. English took that same \emph{bis} in \emph{biscuit}, which is \emph{bis coctus}, \textquotedblleft{}twice cooked,\textquotedblright{} and in \emph{bicycle} and \emph{binary}.

So the word for the oldest person in the room is built out of the number two.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four kinship words, and the -o/-a switch is starting to feel automatic.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la abuela}
  \item \emph{el abuelo y la abuela}
  \item \emph{la abuela y la hija}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{bis} mean? (Twice.) So what is a \emph{bisabuela}? (A great-grandmother.) What is a \emph{biscuit} literally? (Twice cooked.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el esposo]{el esposo --- the one who promised}

\label{lesson:ES-C306-esposo}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time, before anything new is added.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Say it once slowly, then at speed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el esposo} --- \textquotedblleft{}the husband.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{spondere} meant to pledge, to promise in a way that binds. The pledged person was the \textbf{sponsus}. English took the same word twice: once quietly as \emph{spouse}, and once openly as \emph{sponsor} --- somebody who makes a promise on your behalf.

The verb went further than that. To \emph{respond} is to pledge back. To be \emph{despondent} is to have pledged away, given up. All of it is one Latin verb about promises.

And look at the front of the Spanish word. Latin \emph{sponsus} began with s- plus a consonant, and Spanish cannot start a word that way, so it glued an \textbf{e-} on the front: \emph{esposo}. That is the same e- you already have in \emph{España} and \emph{escuela}. The husband is, in the plainest possible terms, the one who promised.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word for a person that is really a word for a promise --- and the chapter's last.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el esposo}
  \item \emph{el esposo y el hijo}
  \item \emph{el nombre del esposo, por favor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{spondere} mean? (To pledge.) Name two English words from it. (\emph{Spouse}, \emph{sponsor}, \emph{respond}, \emph{despondent}.) Why the e- on the front? (Spanish will not start a word with s- plus a consonant.)
\end{tcolorbox}
